comparison: Both evaluate PIM1/2 expression kinetics during T cell activation (C1-C8). OpenEval emphasizes temporal dynamics and data quality. Peer review confirms these findings explicitly, with Reviewer 1 noting PIM1 induction within 3 hours and sustained expression. Peer review also includes Pim3 absence claims (C9-C11) which OpenEval addresses separately in R2.

OpenEval R2 addresses Pim3 absence (C9-C11) with supporting RNAseq/proteomics data. Peer review R1 includes these claims in their broader evaluation of PIM expression patterns but does not specifically comment on Pim3, focusing instead on PIM1/2.

Perfect alignment on Pim dKO mouse characterization (C13-C16). Both accept the reduced splenocyte numbers and body size interpretation. OpenEval notes the inference about body size is reasonable despite lack of direct measurements; peer review accepts this without concern.

Strong agreement on TCR/CD28 activation findings (C17-C23). Both conclude PIM kinases are dispensable for TCR-driven responses. OpenEval emphasizes multiple orthogonal approaches; peer review explicitly quotes the compensation by other signaling pathways. Peer review R3 also includes some IL-2 proliferation claims (C26-C30) not in OpenEval R4.

OpenEval R5 addresses discrepancy with Fox et al. regarding proliferation (C24-C27, C30). Peer review R3 includes these claims in broader TCR activation evaluation but does not specifically discuss the Fox et al. discrepancy, focusing on compensation mechanisms.

OpenEval R6 covers PIM expression in cytokine conditions (C31-C33) as context for IL-15 experiments. Peer review R4 addresses the broader IL-15 findings but includes these contextual claims without specific commentary on the western blot data.

OpenEval R7 addresses modest IL-15 proliferation defect (C34-C36). Peer review R4 encompasses these claims in comprehensive IL-15 evaluation, with Reviewer 1 noting PIM kinases are dispensable for IL-15 programs despite the mild proliferative difference.

Both evaluate IL-15 transcriptional programs (C37-C43). OpenEval emphasizes filtering approach and lack of transcriptional control. Peer review R4 includes these in broader conclusion that PIM kinases don't drive IL-15 metabolic/differentiation programs, accepting the findings without challenge.

Both address IL-15 proteomics and mitochondrial analysis (C44-C49). OpenEval highlights importance of mitochondrial analysis given IL-15's role. Peer review R4 encompasses these findings, with Reviewer 2 noting surprise that PIM1/2 don't influence memory differentiation despite upregulation.

Perfect alignment on IL-2 vs IL-15 differential PIM1 expression and IL-2 proliferation effects (C50-C56). Both accept the mild proliferative defect in IL-2 conditions. OpenEval notes contrast with more pronounced IL-15 effect; peer review accepts findings without criticism.

Both address sustained CD62L expression and reduced size/granularity (C57-C58). OpenEval emphasizes this as striking phenotype suggesting altered trafficking. Peer review R6 includes these in comprehensive trafficking evaluation with explicit confirmation of sustained CD62L in Pim dKO cells.

Both evaluate IL-2 proteomics showing quantitative differences while retaining effector characteristics (C59-C64). OpenEval emphasizes importance for interpreting functional significance. Peer review R7 focuses more on the reduced expression of specific proteins (glucose transporters, effector molecules) covered in OpenEval R13.

Strong agreement on reduced expression of glucose transporters, metabolic proteins, and effector molecules (C65-C71). Both emphasize proteomics data and validation approaches. OpenEval highlights pharmacological inhibitor convergence; peer review explicitly lists affected protein categories and accepts findings as robust.

Both address mTORc1 connection and glucose sensitivity (C72-C73). OpenEval provides mechanistic context through comparison with published mTORc1 inhibition data. Peer review R10 accepts these findings as mechanistic insight explaining proteome changes.

Both evaluate reduced mTORc1 activity in Pim dKO cells (C74-C76). OpenEval emphasizes specificity of mTORc1-dependent vs RSK-mediated phosphorylation. Peer review R10 accepts data showing reduced mTORc1 activity markers as supporting PIM kinases acting upstream/parallel to mTORc1.

Both address KLF2-mediated transcriptional mechanism for homing receptor expression (C77-C81). OpenEval emphasizes established knowledge and coordinate upregulation of KLF2 targets. Peer review R6 includes these claims in comprehensive trafficking evaluation with explicit confirmation.

Strong agreement on adoptive transfer experiments demonstrating altered trafficking (C82-C86). Both emphasize functional validation of molecular findings. OpenEval highlights this as key functional consequence; peer review explicitly confirms PIM1/2KO cells homed better to secondary lymphoid tissue.

Both evaluate major conclusions about context-dependent PIM function (C87-C89). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive dataset support and context-dependency as key insight. Peer review calls findings 'important' and 'thorough and solid,' highlighting proteome vs transcriptome control and IL-2 signaling mediation.

OpenEval R19 addresses PIM kinases mediating IL-2 control of effector proteins (C90-C91). Peer review R12 includes C91 in broader conclusions about PIM kinases shaping effector proteomes, accepting the mechanistic role.

Both address mRNA/protein discordance and reduced protein synthesis (C92-C95). OpenEval emphasizes OPP incorporation assays and modest magnitude acknowledgment. Peer review particularly highlights the 'neat' approach of parallel RNA-seq/proteomics revealing translational control, with editor noting proteomics reveals impact better than transcriptomics.

OpenEval R21 addresses mechanistic model involving reduced mTORc1 and increased PDCD4 (C96-C97). Peer review R9 includes C96 in comprehensive translational control evaluation, accepting the mechanistic model linking PIM kinases to protein synthesis control.

Both synthesize homing receptor findings with functional validation (C98-C102). OpenEval emphasizes integration of molecular and functional data. Peer review R6 explicitly confirms the trafficking phenotype and in vivo validation, accepting conclusion that PIM kinases mediate IL-2 repression of naive trafficking program.

Perfect alignment on clarification that lymph node homing doesn't reflect complete memory differentiation (C103-C106). Both emphasize this addresses alternative interpretation. OpenEval highlights PCA analysis; peer review accepts nuanced interpretation distinguishing impaired effector differentiation from memory conversion.

Both address translational/clinical context for PIM kinase research (C107-C108). OpenEval emphasizes establishing clinical relevance. Peer review R14 includes these claims and notes translational link through small molecule inhibitors, accepting clinical relevance as important aspect.

Perfect alignment on explaining discrepancies with prior work and context-dependent function (C109-C113). Both accept differential PIM expression doesn't predict function. OpenEval synthesizes with James et al. findings; peer review explicitly notes surprise about cell-type specific effects and accepts authors' explanation.

OpenEval R26 addresses reduced mTORc1 activity (C114) and context-dependent PIM function synthesis (C115). Peer review R10 accepts mTORc1 findings as mechanistic insight. C115 is also addressed in peer review R12 as important conceptual advance.

OpenEval R26 synthesizes context-dependent PIM function (C115) as conceptual advance. Peer review R12 accepts this as important finding about differential requirements across TCR, IL-15, and IL-2 conditions, with Reviewer 2 noting hints toward general finding about kinase behavior in different T cell states.

Strong agreement on parallel RNAseq/proteomics revealing post-transcriptional regulation (C116-C122). OpenEval emphasizes rigorous quantitative analysis. Peer review particularly praises the 'neat' matched approach uncovering translational control, with editor highlighting proteomics superiority over transcriptomics for revealing PIM impact.

Strong agreement on translational control mechanism through PDCD4/EIF4A1 (C123-C130). OpenEval emphasizes converging evidence from multiple approaches. Peer review accepts comprehensive mechanistic analysis, with Reviewer 2 particularly liking matched RNA-seq/proteomics approach, though noting OPP assay used inhibitors not knockout cells.

OpenEval R29 addresses established knowledge about PIM kinase regulation (C131-C134) providing study context. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though this background is implicitly accepted in peer review discussions.

OpenEval R30 addresses prior literature citations (C135-C139) establishing knowledge base and areas of agreement/disagreement. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers reference some of this literature in their assessments.

Both address translational context and clinical implications (C140-C145). OpenEval emphasizes therapeutic development importance and benefits/risks of PIM inhibition. Peer review R14 accepts translational relevance, with Reviewer 2 noting small molecule inhibitor experiments provide translational link given potential clinical use.
